title: Beating the drum for rainbow recruits: Police have done all they can
article: Short of forming roving press gangs as the old British sea captains did to snatch people off the street to make up a ship's crew, there's not a lot more Calgary police can do to encourage minorities to join the force.

As happens periodically with police forces across Canada, this week Calgary's finest were talking again about the need to recruit minorities to, as Insp. Barry Clark put it, "reflect the growing population in the city."

That's nice, but really, what is there left for the police to do? For years, the police have been speaking to minority community meetings, reaching out to minority students at school presentations, holding job fairs and advertising in local ethnic newspapers.

"The chief is out all the time," says police spokesman Don Stewart, ticking off a partial list of community functions Chief Jack Beaton has attended recently, including meetings with a local Grenadian-Canadian group, as well as Vietnamese Calgarians.

Maybe it's time Beaton said, "OK, people. We've done our part. Time for you to do yours." In other words, whether you're black, white, red, yellow or purple polka-dot, if you want to be a police officer, go sign up. On the other hand, if throngs of Grenadians, Laotians or for that matter, Norwegians (at just over 26,000, they certainly are a minority in this city,) do not rush to enrol in the next recruit class, the police need to accept that the interest simply isn't there.

That's because you can't expect people to make career choices based on their ethnic origins. If the Calgary police suddenly decided they needed more Jewish women on the force, they wouldn't be hearing from me. My career interests, like most people's, have nothing to do with my ethnic background. If they did, I would have become a rabbi.

And frankly, I don't care about the ethnicity of the cop who comes to my aid when I need the police. I can't envision phoning 911 in the middle of the night and saying, "Somebody's trying to break into my house. Could you send a cop who's Jewish? And, oh yeah, could you make sure he keeps kosher, too?" I just want the police to get there quickly and deal with the situation -- and I think it's safe to say that's what every Calgarian, regardless of ethnic persuasion, wants.

The police say the latest talk about minority recruitment has nothing to do with the recent fatal shooting of Sudanese immigrant Deng Kuol. That is as it should be. Those who are grumbling about racism might want to explain what Const. Ira Macumber was supposed to do when Kuol came at him with a knife. Should he have graciously allowed himself to perish, just to keep the multicultural peace? The fact is, whether your name is Deng Kuol or Ole Oleson, if you attack a police officer, you're likely to pay for it with your life.

A few years ago, there was a mercifully short-lived movement afoot elsewhere in Canada to specially recruit gay firefighters. It fizzled out because there wasn't a single incident of anyone leaning from the window of a burning building shouting at the firefighters holding the net: "I won't jump if you're not lesbians!"

Nor does EMS come under the kind of pressure to recruit minorities that the police do. EMS spokesman Mike Plato says that's because anyone who wants to be a paramedic has to be trained first and certified by the Alberta College of Paramedics before applying for a job.
"We hire people with four years of education. The police recruit people for on-the-job training," Plato says.
I suspect another reason is that when you're having a heart attack, the ethnic background of the paramedic who shows up to save you isn't exactly a top priority.
Calgary police should focus on capturing the bad guys. The good guys will come to them of their own accord.
